name: Moss-Null
specific_features: Automated beacon (distress, navigation, or unknown purpose)
description: Moss-Null is barely a world. This tiny barren planetoid, smaller than most moons, orbits at the outer edge of its system in a trajectory that takes centuries to complete. Its surface is a uniform dark grey, pocked with ancient craters and smoothed by eons of solar wind erosion into gentle undulations that, from certain angles, resemble the rounded cushions of moss growing on stone. The negligible gravity means that a careless step can achieve escape velocity, and the surface dust barely clings to the rock beneath.

There is nothing to recommend Moss-Null to any visitor. The airless surface offers no shelter, no resources of note, and no view worth the journey to see it. The sun is a bright star among many, providing enough light to see by but no warmth, and the temperature varies only by the slow rotation that exposes each face alternately to starlight and shadow. The experience of standing on Moss-Null is the experience of standing on nothing, a rock too small to matter in a system too empty to notice.

An automated beacon orbits Moss-Null at close range, placed there by a survey mission that used the planetoid as a reference point for deep-space calibration measurements. The beacon broadcasts a standard navigational signal on a frequency rarely monitored, and its power source will exhaust itself within the next decade. When it falls silent, nothing will mark Moss-Null's location in any active system, and the planetoid will return to the anonymity it never really left. The beacon's placement was an accident of convenience, not an endorsement of significance.

Moss-Null exists at the boundary between object and place. It is too small to appear on most navigation charts, too remote to encounter by accident, and too resource-poor to justify a deliberate visit. Its iron content is negligible, its scientific interest is nil, and its aesthetic appeal is limited to those who find beauty in absolute desolation. Yet it persists, as it has for billions of years, a tiny knot of matter in the vast emptiness, asking nothing and offering nothing in return. Some travelers find that more compelling than any wonder.
